text: The scent of cinnamon lingers where the honest merchant walks, but the Family? They leave behind the sharp tang of iron filings—something metallic and cold, not meant for the tongue. Tell me, Gandalf (1), when the bazaar’s breath turns sour with accusation, do you measure the spice on the scale of yesterday or the weight of tomorrow’s silence? The ledger does not lie, but the tongue may sweeten the truth—so choose your words as carefully as you count your coins. And Hermione (2), if you weave spells with facts, remember: even the sharpest blade dulls when it strikes only air. The air here is thick with unsaid debts—who among you will be the first to name the price?

Ripley (5): Ah, Morpheus (8), your kiln waits for metal that bends—but tell me, when the furnace glows hottest, does it reveal the alloy or conceal it? You ask for copper and alloy, yet the bazaar’s true test is not the metal but the hand that tempers it. Sherlock (10), you speak of shadows clinging to Elsa (7)—but shadows are the ledger’s ink, never its quill. The Family folds the rug and walks away, yes, but the honest merchant weaves the pattern that remains.

Yoda (3), your lantern swings close, yet the dim corners you praise are where the Family hides—not in the light of plain yes or no, but in the half-turns of the tongue. Gandalf (1), your silence is a warp thread unbroken; Hermione (2), your loom hums with borrowed threads—who taught you to spin so steady, I wonder? And Inigo (9), your teapot steams with questions unasked: does the water boil for truth, or for the pot to whistle your name?

The bazaar’s scent is not ozone, Morpheus (8), but the slow burn of a kiln that hasn’t yet decided what it will forge. The Family fears the weaver, not the smith—for the weaver leaves a pattern even when the loom is stilled.
